dedupe_keys.name: queensland ward level discrete event simulation of strategies to reduce emergency access block at three large hospitals

description: This case study uses discrete event simulation to test ways of reducing access block, the delay in moving admitted emergency patients to a ward, at three principal referral public hospitals in Queensland, Australia. The team, from CSIRO's Australian e-Health Research Centre, the University of Queensland, Queensland hospitals and the Queensland Ambulance Service, built and validated ward-level models from every emergency department presentation, inpatient episode and ward movement between 1 September 2021 and 31 August 2022, and published the results in an open-access journal article. Outcomes were emergency department length of stay, waiting time, access block rate, four-hour rule compliance and bed use. Coverage is three hospitals over one year. The article is free under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives licence; the hospital data are not public. Caveats: results apply to large metropolitan hospitals and the modelled strategies are idealised. The study found that removing maintenance care patients from hospital could cut access block by up to a third, that earlier-in-the-day discharges and sharing patients among wards brought large gains, and that diverting general practitioner type patients had negligible effect. Simulation uses: evidence and calibration targets for hospital capacity and patient flow models. Related records: the treatment centre simulation model (model-treat-sim-treatment-centre-des) is an open discrete event model of a similar process.
